bp: A Telegram post is not only a message; it is a seed for a possible conversation. Moderators, channel owners, and communication tools often need to know whether that seed is likely to grow into support, joking, conflict, hostile replies, or toxic argument. The difficulty is timing: the comments that reveal the audience reaction may not exist yet, or they may be unavailable to the system that must make an early decision. EmoTg serves that early-warning moment. It asks whether the post itself contains enough visible clues to anticipate the social response it will attract. The real-world use is proactive moderation and risk assessment: instead of waiting until a comment thread becomes harmful, the system tries to estimate likely thread behavior from the original message's language, style, topic, and emotional tone. The paper therefore treats content as a source of social forecast, not merely as text to classify in isolation.
wh: The hard part is that audience reaction is not written directly inside the post. A post may look calm but invite conflict because it touches a divisive stance. Another post may use sharp words but be understood as humor by its audience. Without comments, the system has only the initial message, so it must infer a missing future response from indirect signs. Simple text cues are also incomplete. Word choice, style, topic, sentiment, emotional framing, and implied stance can all matter at once, and each may point in a different direction. The abstract says the paper handles several targets at the same time, including sentiment, toxicity, stance, humor, and conflict. That makes the task harder than a single harmful-versus-safe label. The system must learn which post features predict which kind of response, while recognizing that the same post can be cute in one dimension and risky in another.
naive: A smart beginner might build a keyword filter for Telegram posts. It would mark posts with insults, threats, or loaded political words as risky, and treat posts without those words as safe. That fails because social reaction depends on more than banned words. Toxic comments can follow a post whose wording is polite but whose stance invites attack. Humor can soften language that looks negative on the surface. Conflict may arise from the relationship between topic, style, and emotional framing rather than from one phrase. Another beginner might wait for comments and classify the thread after the fact. That gives better evidence, but it arrives too late for proactive moderation. EmoTg is aimed exactly at the gap between those two simple choices: keyword rules are too shallow, and comment-based judgment is delayed or unavailable.
ap: The core idea is to turn each Telegram post into a richer set of measurable clues, then learn how those clues map to likely comment-thread behavior. The paper uses two feature sources. Standard natural-language processing supplies more mechanical signals from the raw message, such as linguistic and stylistic properties. GPT-based structured prompts, meaning carefully specified questions asked of a language model, extract higher-level semantic and emotional descriptions. Separately, comments are annotated with another dedicated prompt to create thread-level labels for sentiment, toxicity, stance, humor, conflict, and related reactions. Those labels become the answers the model learns to predict. The post-to-comment task is then framed as multi-task classification: one input post is used to predict several response attributes. XGBoost, a tree-based learning method that combines many small rule-like splits, learns which combinations of post features are associated with each audience reaction.
mech: The mechanism starts with raw Telegram messages. First, the pipeline reads the post text and extracts ordinary language features: visible wording, stylistic patterns, and other natural-language signals available before anyone replies. Second, it sends structured prompts to a GPT-style language model. A structured prompt is not an open-ended request for a summary; it asks for specific properties so the answers can become consistent fields, such as semantic meaning, emotional tone, or style. Third, the pipeline handles the response side independently. Existing comments are annotated with a dedicated prompt, producing thread-level labels that summarize how the audience responded: sentiment, toxicity, stance, humor, conflict, and emotional attributes such as cuteness. Fourth, the system pairs each post's feature record with the labels derived from its comment thread. This creates training examples where the input is only the post, but the target is the later or separate audience response. Fifth, XGBoost trains several classifiers over the same post features. Each classifier is built from decision trees, where each tree asks a sequence of feature questions and votes on a label. Combining many trees lets the model capture feature interactions without requiring one hand-written rule. The output is a set of predicted response labels for a new post, plus SHAP-based explanations showing which features pushed particular predictions.
math: The main mathematical idea is supervised classification under uncertainty. Supervised means the system receives examples with inputs and target labels: here, post features are the inputs, and comment-thread labels are the targets. Classification means choosing among named outcomes, such as toxic or not toxic, conflict or not conflict, and other response attributes. Multi-task classification adds a practical twist: the same post representation is used to predict several related labels, because a thread's emotional shape is not one number. XGBoost supplies the scoring machinery. A decision tree divides examples by asking simple feature questions; boosting builds many such trees in sequence so later trees focus on mistakes left by earlier ones. In everyday terms, it repeatedly asks, "Which remaining distinction would reduce wrong guesses most?" SHAP explainability uses a contribution idea from cooperative game theory, where the model asks how much each feature changes the prediction when considered across many possible feature combinations. That fits this paper because a social response rarely comes from one cue alone. The tradeoff is predictive power versus interpretability: many trees can capture subtle combinations, but SHAP is needed to show which linguistic, stylistic, semantic, or emotional clues mattered.
dots: EmoTg sits between several recurring conference ideas. It is a text-mining paper because it turns messy language into decision-ready evidence, but it is not only about the words in one document. It is also a social-response paper: the target is how a crowd may react, which connects it to broader social-network and platform-safety work where posts, comments, and users form feedback loops. It neighbors stance detection because both ask how position and framing can be inferred from language; in this case, stance is one of the response labels rather than the only output. It neighbors toxicity and moderation work because the practical value is earlier risk detection before harm spreads through replies. It also belongs with explainability papers because the abstract emphasizes SHAP and behaviorally meaningful language-model-derived features. The common deeper problem is evidence assignment: when a platform makes a socially important prediction, it must say which cues supported the warning rather than leaving moderators with a black-box score.
ww: The approach can work when post content and audience response are statistically tied in repeated Telegram examples. A message carries more than topic. It carries stance, emotional temperature, style, implied audience, and cues about whether it invites agreement, joking, attack, or dispute. If many past posts with similar cues produced similar comment labels, a model can learn those regularities and apply them to a new post before comments arrive. Combining standard language features with GPT-derived structured features helps because the two sources catch different evidence. Mechanical text features can notice visible patterns that are easy to count. Prompt-derived features can name higher-level meaning and emotion that a keyword list would miss. XGBoost is a reasonable fit because it can learn interactions: a feature may matter only when paired with another feature. SHAP then supports trust by translating the trained model's decision back into feature contributions. The abstract's reported accuracies, up to 0.85 for emotional attributes and 0.71 for toxic comment prediction, suggest that the post contains useful but imperfect signals.
po: The payoff is an early estimate of likely audience behavior when comments are absent or not yet available. For moderation, that means a platform or channel manager can prioritize risky posts before a comment thread becomes toxic or conflict-heavy. For socially aware AI support, it means a writing or publishing tool could warn that a post's wording may invite a harmful reaction and show which features drive that concern. The abstract grounds the result in Telegram data and reports strong performance for emotional attributes such as cuteness and conflict, plus usable but lower accuracy for toxic comment prediction. The SHAP analysis adds a second payoff: the system can offer inspectable reasons rather than only a label.
limits: The claims depend on the Telegram data, the prompt-generated labels, and the stability of the relationship between posts and comments. If another community reacts differently to the same wording, the learned mapping may fail. The abstract does not prove that GPT annotations perfectly match human judgment for sentiment, toxicity, stance, humor, or conflict. It also does not show that post content alone captures audience composition, timing, moderation history, or external events that shape replies. Accuracy for toxic comment prediction is notably lower than for some emotional attributes, so high-stakes use should keep human review. SHAP explanations show feature influence inside the trained model, not guaranteed real-world causes of audience behavior.
